content: The review identified two cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) and two non-randomized studies (NRSs) conducted in moderate to high malaria transmission settings across four countries: Burkina Faso, Gambia, Nigeria, and Zambia. These studies assessed the impact of mass drug administration (MDA) on Plasmodium falciparum transmission compared to no MDA. The results were categorized into three time periods: 1–3 months, 4–12 months, and 12–24 months after the last round of MDA. The cRCTs and NRSs were analyzed and graded separately using the GRADE approach. The findings below report absolute effects (risk differences) of the intervention, as these were used by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) in their judgments. Relative effect sizes are available in the research evidence. Immediate to Short-Term Benefits (1–3 months after the last MDA round): MDA may result in little to no difference in P. falciparum prevalence (Risk Difference [RD]: 38 cases per 1000 persons; 95% Confidence Interval [CI]: -21 to 219 per 1000 persons; one cRCT; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of MDA on P. falciparum prevalence (RD: -108 per 1000 persons; 95% CI: -159 to -51 per 1000 persons; one NRS; very low-certainty evidence). MDA probably reduces the incidence of P. falciparum parasitemia (RD: -22 per 1000 person-years; 95% CI: -34 to -5 per 1000 person-years; one cRCT; moderate-certainty evidence). MDA may result in little to no difference in the incidence of P. falciparum clinical malaria (RD: -1 per 1000 person-years; 95% CI: -2 to 8 per 1000 person-years; one cRCT; low-certainty evidence). Medium-Term Benefits (4–12 months after the last MDA round): MDA may result in little to no difference in P. falciparum prevalence (RD: -87 per 1000 persons; 95% CI: -53 to 271 per 1000 persons; one cRCT; low-certainty evidence). MDA may reduce P. falciparum prevalence (RD: -167 per 1000 persons; 95% CI: -188 to -138 per 1000 persons; one NRS; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of MDA on the incidence of P. falciparum parasitemia (RD: -10 per 1000 person-years; 95% CI: -49 to 54 per 1000 person-years; one cRCT; very low-certainty evidence). Long-Term Benefits (12–24 months after the last MDA round): MDA may reduce P. falciparum prevalence (RD: -99 per 1000 person-years; 95% CI: -129 to -69 per 1000 person-years; one NRS; low-certainty evidence). Adverse Events: The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of MDA on adverse events (RD: 200 per 1000 persons; 95% CI: -39 to 572 per 1000 persons; one cRCT; very low-certainty evidence). GDG Judgments: The GDG noted the challenges in assessing the effect of MDA on P. falciparum in moderate to high transmission settings due to the limited number of studies and the overall very low certainty of evidence. They judged that both the desirable and undesirable effects of MDA were small, and the balance of effects likely did not favor MDA for reducing P. falciparum transmission in these settings. Additionally, the GDG expressed concerns that any impact of MDA would likely be short-lived in moderate to high transmission settings. The overall certainty of evidence was judged to be very low. Values and Preferences: No studies were identified regarding preferences and values. The GDG judged that there might be significant uncertainty or variability in preferences or values, which could not be determined due to the lack of studies. Resources: The systematic review identified four studies with information on resource needs for MDA. The estimated cost was $40 per person per round, with one study reporting that drugs accounted for 70% of the total cost. Compared to reactive drug administration (RDA), MDA was superior in all cost-effectiveness measures, including cost per infection averted, cost per case averted, cost per death averted, and cost per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted. However, the GDG judged that the resources required to implement MDA were substantial and could negatively impact the implementation of other recommended malaria prevention strategies. They also found it difficult to judge the cost-effectiveness of MDA due to the very low certainty of evidence and the variability in effectiveness and cost depending on the time period over which they are measured. Equity: The systematic review did not identify any research addressing how MDA affects health equity. The GDG judged that the impact of implementing MDA on equity would vary. While MDA has the potential to reach populations with limited access to other malaria prevention and treatment services, it also exposes uninfected individuals to potential adverse effects of antimalarials. The GDG felt that MDA could exacerbate inequity if not implemented appropriately or if the intervention resulted in only a small, temporary effect. Acceptability: The systematic review identified 18 studies providing information on the acceptability of MDA. The most common barrier to acceptability was fear of adverse events. Some participants expressed concerns that adverse events from MDA might inhibit their economic productivity, although others felt that malaria infection was more likely to limit economic activity than adverse events. Sensitization about the benefits of MDA and providing healthcare to participating communities helped reduce concerns about adverse effects. However, the presence of expatriate physicians, ambulances, and unfamiliar informed consent processes sometimes elevated concerns. Previous experiences with MDA influenced community perceptions, with poor experiences leading to negative impressions. In areas where other malaria interventions had been effectively implemented, MDA was viewed more positively. The GDG judged that the acceptability of MDA depended on whether factors affecting community and individual acceptance were appropriately addressed in the intervention design. Feasibility: The systematic review identified 13 studies on the feasibility of implementing MDA. Barriers included residents’ absence during campaigns, seasonal mobility, and challenges in determining the optimal timing of campaigns due to weather, agricultural activities, religious events, and policy changes. Feasibility was improved in smaller populations and island communities. The GDG judged that the feasibility of implementing MDA varied depending on the size of the population to be covered. Practical Considerations for P. vivax: MDA without an 8-aminoquinoline medicine may have a short-term (1–3 months) impact on P. vivax transmission. For MDA to contribute meaningfully to malaria elimination, it must be part of a robust program that includes case-based surveillance, quality-assured parasitological diagnosis, effective antimalarial treatment (including treatment for hypnozoites), and additional prevention strategies. MDA should be implemented in areas with limited risk of malaria importation and during periods of low population movement to maximize coverage and reduce the risk of resurgence. Achieving high population coverage and adherence to the full therapeutic course is critical for the success of MDA programs.
